items.title: Anthropic's S-1: $518B of infrastructure over a decade, 80% non-cancellable
items.idea: Anthropic's S-1 says it expects to spend $518B on AI infrastructure over ten years, and 80% of that is non-cancellable: payments are owed whatever it actually uses. It also says the business will be 'principally limited by the availability of compute', so spend could pass $1T. NERC's 10-year peak US power demand projection is 245 GW.
items.angle: A frontier lab is now carrying take-or-pay obligations like a utility or an airline. That moves AI capex risk from 'optional growth spend' to 'fixed charge', which matters for the credit angle on the neoclouds and the lessors.
items.tweetA: Anthropic's S-1: $518B over ten years, 80% non-cancellable. That is not a growth budget, that is a fixed charge. Revenue has to compound just to service the take-or-pay. Who sits on the other side of those contracts? $ORCL $CRWV $NVDA
items.tweetB: 245 GW of US peak demand growth in NERC's 10-year view. One lab alone plans $518B of compute. Utilities plan in decades, model labs in quarters. The mismatch gets priced somewhere, and I think it shows up in power equities before it shows up in model pricing.

charts.desc: a16z chart: about 20% of invested AI capex goes to power

items.title: 800VDC: if racks stop at 200-250 kW, what happens to the power-semi thesis?
items.idea: Today's racks run about 200 kW on 48/50V DC. Doubling chip count would push distribution past 10,000 A, which is infeasible, hence 800VDC. A principal NVIDIA engineer told Vik racks may not go beyond 200-250 kW because cooling and power delivery outweigh the benefits. With eight Oberon racks in a 576-GPU domain at Rubin Ultra, the question is whether MW-class racks are needed at all.
items.angle: The bull case for SiC/GaN names assumed rack power keeps scaling. If it plateaus, 800VDC and sidecar designs still help, but the content-per-rack growth slows. Worth separating the 'voltage' story from the 'wattage' story.
items.tweetA: Everyone underwrites 800VDC on MW racks. An NVIDIA engineer says racks may top out at 200-250 kW. If so, you still need higher voltage, but the content-per-rack growth story is half as big. Which names have priced the wrong one? $ON $NVTS $WOLF
items.tweetB: At 48V, a 1 MW rack needs over 20,000 A. Copper does not scale like transistors. The AI buildout is increasingly a bus bar problem, and bus bars are bought by people who do not care about your model benchmark.

items.title: AI financing is moving off balance sheet: Amazon $8B GPU leaseback, $60B Broadcom-linked Anthropic structure
items.idea: Amazon is reportedly exploring moving about $8B of Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs into an SPV, with outside investors owning the chips and Amazon leasing them back. Separately, Broadcom-linked financing for Anthropic and others is heading toward a $60B structure with a large senior secured bank tranche and Blackstone lower in the stack. The author's risk case needs no bust, only growth that stops accelerating while structures priced on scarcity and generous residual values multiply.
items.angle: Residual value of a GPU is the whole game in a leaseback. Snider's piece in the same batch (bridge debt on Oracle's Jupiter site at 88-90c) shows what happens when utilization breaks. This is the 2000 telecom vendor-financing rhyme.
items.tweetA: Amazon wants outside money to own $8B of Blackwells and lease them back. When a hyperscaler with enormous operating cash flow moves chips off balance sheet, the signal is not that it is out of money. It is that it prefers not to carry the residual. $AMZN $NVDA $BX
items.tweetB: Senior secured tranche at the banks, Blackstone below it, Anthropic as the end user. That is a 2007 CLO diagram with GPUs as collateral. The question nobody can answer yet: what is a 3-year-old H100 worth if training demand shifts?

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Goldman (Chris Lucas)
items.title: ETFs: $1.5T in three quarters, about $8B per session, Goldman sees $2T+ for 2026
items.idea: More than $1.5T has gone into the ETF complex in the first three quarters of 2026, already above last year's record, which works out to roughly $167B a month or $8B per trading day. Goldman's Lucas expects $2T+ of US ETF inflows. MAGS has persistent inflows while equal-weight RSP struggles, TLT is at historic lows and still draws flow, and fixed-income ETF volume rises with rates volatility.
items.angle: ETF creation/redemption is now a primary transmission channel: bond-market stress shows up in TLT volume, concentration shows up in MAGS flows. A $8B/day bid is also what holds the index near records while breadth is terrible.
items.tweetA: $8B a day into ETFs, $1.5T in nine months. MAGS gets bought, RSP gets sold, TLT hits all-time lows and still gets bought. The marginal buyer is not looking at valuation at all. That is a flow regime, not a valuation regime, and it ends when the flow does.
items.tweetB: Long-duration bond ETFs are being bought at historic lows while the 30-year sits at its highest since 2002. Either that is the contrarian trade of the decade, or tax-loss harvesting is propping up the volume. Check which one before you size it. $TLT $MAGS $RSP

items.title: China is exporting inflation: export prices +11.6% y/y, import prices +21.0%
items.idea: China's export prices rose 11.6% y/y in July after years of deflation, advanced Asia export prices are up 21.6%, and China's import prices are up 21.0% on chips, crude, copper and iron ore. Terms of trade are deteriorating even as export prices rise, which squeezes Chinese margins. Retail inventories were ordered months ago, so pass-through to consumers is still ahead.
items.angle: The disinflation-from-China leg of the post-2001 goods price story is reversing. Bianco's note in the David Lin issue (goods CPI -0.5%/yr 2001-2020 vs about +2%/yr now) is the same trend seen from the US side.
items.tweetA: For 20 years China exported disinflation. Export prices now +11.6% y/y, import prices +21.0%. Margins get squeezed at the source, pass-through comes to Western shelves with a lag. Goods inflation was the last thing central banks assumed would stay quiet.
items.tweetB: Bianco: goods prices fell 0.5% a year from 2001 to 2020 and now rise about 2%. BMO: China's export prices +11.6%. Put those together and the structural disinflation trade, long duration, long retail margins, is the wrong side.

items.title: 30Y UST at 5.61% (highest since 2002), Bund 3.6%, payrolls +29k vs 84-90k expected
items.idea: 30-year Treasury topped 5.61% on Tuesday, the highest since 2002; the 10-year hit about 5.3%; Germany's 10-year topped 3.6%, highest since 2008. Core PCE held at 3.0% versus a 3.3% forecast and September payrolls came in at +29k against 84-90k expected, with July revised to -10k. October hike odds fell from about 70% to 17%, but December stayed above 75%. Consumer confidence is at 81.9, lowest since 2014.
items.angle: Weak jobs, soft PCE, and yet the 10-year ends the week at 5.28% because oil rebounds. The curve is being driven by supply and hike expectations, not growth.
items.tweetA: Payrolls +29k, July negative, core PCE under forecast, and the 10-year still closes the week near 5.3%. Bad data is not rallying bonds anymore. That tells you what is driving the long end: supply, not growth.
items.tweetB: December hike odds above 75% with payrolls at +29k. Warsh either hikes into a labor market that has stopped adding jobs or tells the bond market he won't. Both outcomes are volatility. $TLT $DXY

charts.desc: Weekly recap; charts likely in video/article

items.title: Hanke: Divisia M4 at 7.4% and AI credit demand are creating money while the Fed hikes
items.idea: Divisia M4 is growing 7.4% a year versus 5.6% a year earlier; Hanke puts the growth consistent with 2% inflation at about 6%. Hot AI-firm credit demand makes banks lend, and the resulting deposits count as money, so money keeps growing even as the Fed hikes. AI equity and debt issuance is above $1T, matching all other issuance a few years ago. He calls the bond move a 'buyer strike' and only likes TIPS.
items.angle: The mechanism is new: AI capex is the credit impulse that offsets tight policy. If the AI financing channel narrows (see the off-balance-sheet and Oracle bridge-debt items), money growth, and with it the cushion under the economy, turns down fast.
items.tweetA: Divisia M4 at 7.4% while the Fed hikes. The reason is AI: banks lend to data center borrowers, the loans create deposits, deposits are money. The AI buildout is a monetary policy offset. When it slows, so does the cushion under the whole economy.
items.tweetB: Hanke calls it a bond-buyer strike, not a run: investors simply refuse new Treasuries below a higher yield. A strike ends when the price is right. The question is how much further the price has to go before the auctions clear.

items.source: David Lin Report / Rory Johnston (Commodity Context)
items.title: Hormuz at about 14 mb/d but 7 mb/d still missing; transit cost above $30/bbl vs $2 prewar
items.idea: Johnston: about 14 mb/d now pass Hormuz, up from 5-6 mb/d a month and a half ago, but roughly 7 mb/d still do not. Supply has been in deficit six to seven months, so a smaller deficit moves prices more than a larger one did in March-April because buffers are gone. Transit likely costs more than $30/bbl against about $2 before the war. Diesel crack topped $120, leaving diesel at about double crude; Russian diesel exports are near zero.
items.angle: A prompt Brent spread of $5 is 'remarkable' because such spreads are normally cents. Buffers are the story: SPR draws are what's holding the price. G7's 100M bbl pledge over four months is about 0.8 mb/d, small next to 7 mb/d still missing.
items.tweetA: 100M barrels over four months from the G7 is about 0.8 mb/d. Hormuz is still missing about 7 mb/d. The SPR release is a rounding error against the gap. The market knows it, which is why diesel crack is above $120. $VLO $MPC
items.tweetB: Johnston: 500 kb/d of extra Chinese diesel could cut cracks by $30-40/bbl. China holds the world's only underutilized refining capacity. The relief valve for American diesel sits in a country we are in a trade war with. Think about who that gives leverage to.

items.title: Bianco: first time buying bonds since 2020; effective oil price near $200 including tanker and military costs
items.idea: With the 10-year near 5.25%, Bianco says inflation, deficit and supply worries are largely priced and he is looking to buy bonds. The 10-year went from 3.7% to 5% during 175bp of cuts, which he reads as policy being too easy. Last time oil was near $100 the 10-year was 4.40-4.50%. He puts the effective price of oil, including tanker and military costs, near $200. Expected returns: cash 4%, bonds 5%, stocks 6%.
items.angle: Expected returns of 4/5/6 make the equity risk premium roughly 1%. Combine with Hay's CAPE of 41 and Hunter's double-top call on the 10-year: three guests, one trade, long duration.
items.tweetA: Bianco is buying bonds for the first time since 2020. Hunter says the 10-year is double-topping the 2007 high. The same week Hanke says avoid nominals. When three of the most respected macro voices split this cleanly, the 5.3% level is the debate.
items.tweetB: Cash 4%, bonds 5%, stocks 6%. That is a 100bp premium for taking equity risk at a CAPE of 41. You are paid almost nothing to own the most crowded asset class in history. $SPY $TLT

items.source: David Lin Report / Jeff Snider (Eurodollar University)
items.title: Snider: steep front-end/flat back-end curve occurs 5.4% of the time since 1990; Oracle bridge debt at 88-90c
items.idea: Snider: a steep front end with a flat back end has occurred only 5.4% of the time since 1990, with 2s10s at about 19bp, and has appeared only shortly before a recession or a turn to rate cuts. The NY Fed survey's mean probability of unemployment rose to 44.4%, the highest since 2020. After a force majeure at Oracle's Jupiter data center in New Mexico, banks that provided bridge financing hold debt trading near 88-90 cents on the dollar. He calls credit the biggest hurdle for the AI buildout.
items.angle: A named AI datacenter loan trading at 88-90c is the first public price on AI project-finance risk. Pair it with the Amazon SPV and the $60B Broadcom-linked structure: the financing layer is where stress would first show.
items.tweetA: A bridge loan on Oracle's Jupiter data center trades at 88-90 cents after a force majeure. First public mark on AI project credit. Meanwhile banks are lining up a $60B structure for the next one. $ORCL
items.tweetB: Steep front, flat back occurs 5.4% of the time since 1990 and has preceded recession or cuts every time. The market is pricing hikes into that shape. One of those two is wrong, and the curve has the better track record.

items.title: Hay: Shanghai physical at $135 vs WTI $92, US SPR to lowest since 1982, Europe gas $20 vs US $3
items.idea: Hay calls it the worst energy crisis ever: the US is releasing another 40M barrels, bringing the SPR to its lowest since 1982. Shanghai physical hit $135 against about $92 for WTI. Crack spread near $100 against a usual $10-15, diesel at $200/bbl. US gas is about $3/MMBtu versus above $20 in Europe and Asia, with European storage 70% full versus a usual 85%. He sees a good chance of gas lines in California and calls energy stocks a buy on pullbacks: XLE +40% YTD, energy 3.3% of the S&P.
items.angle: The physical/futures gap ($135 vs $92) says paper markets understate scarcity. Europe at 70% storage into winter with $20 gas is the next leg.
items.tweetA: Shanghai physical $135. WTI $92. Same barrel, $43 difference. Futures are telling you about the Western hedge book; physical is telling you about scarcity. Energy is 3.3% of the S&P after a 40% year. $XLE
items.tweetB: US gas $3, Europe and Asia above $20, European storage 70% against 85% normal. The arb is a LNG tanker. The winter is not priced for a country that cannot buy its way out. $LNG $EQT

items.title: Hunter: one more rally (S&P 10,000) then a global bust to 2,000, with the 10-year at a double top
items.idea: Hunter sees S&P 10,000, Nasdaq 36,000, Dow 70,000 within three to six months (30-35% gains), then a bust with stocks down as much as 80% driven by leverage in debt and derivatives, likely starting in 2027, possibly from private credit. He is newly bullish on bonds: the 10-year at 5.3% forms a double top with 2007, with yields below 4% in six months, then 0% in the bust. He sees oil lower in Q4, DXY at low-mid 80s, gold $7,000 and silver $200.
items.angle: A fully consistent 'melt-up then bust' framework, but its three legs (stocks up, yields down, dollar down) conflict with the energy view that yields are driven by supply of money.
items.tweetA: Hunter: S&P 10,000 first, then 2,000. Yields double-top at 5.3%, oil peaks, dollar collapses, gold $7,000. Notice what the forecast needs: the Fed stops hiking, and Hormuz reopens. Both are binary and neither is in his control.
items.tweetB: The most extreme guest this week still thinks stocks go up 30% first. Smead says S&P is lower in 10 years with near certainty. Same market, same week, the range of expert opinion is wider than at any point I can remember.

items.title: Smead: top 20 stocks are 45% of the S&P, Wilshire 5000 at 240% of GDP, homebuilders at 0.8x book
items.idea: Smead says the AI mania is about five times the dot-com boom and the Wilshire 5000 trades at 240% of GDP, with 20 companies making up 45% of the S&P 500. He compares it to 1987, when the Fed cut 200bp the same afternoon. His funds own no tech or AI; his largest US positions are Cenovus and Apache, and he is buying homebuilders at about 0.8x book. Four of the 15 largest listed homebuilders were bought out in five months, including Taylor Morrison by Berkshire.
items.angle: Berkshire buying a homebuilder at 0.8x book is a signal that cheap book value is being picked up by strategic buyers, a different kind of data point from a valuation argument.
items.tweetA: Four of the 15 largest US homebuilders were bought out in five months. Berkshire took Taylor Morrison. Buyers with permanent capital are buying at 0.8x book while the index trades at 240% of GDP. Someone is wrong. $BRK.B
items.tweetB: 20 companies are 45% of the S&P. In 1987 the Fed cut 200bp in an afternoon. If that is the playbook for the next break, bonds in the zero-to-five year bucket are the beneficiary. Smead's trade is the opposite of everyone's current exposure.

items.source: David Lin Report / Nicky Shiels (MKS PAMP)
items.title: Gold: model fair value $3,200 with an $840 debasement premium; +50bp real yields means -$500
items.idea: Shiels says gold near $4,100 sits at an $840/oz premium to a fair value of about $3,200 from a model on 10-year real yields and the DXY. Real yields are back to 2007 levels; another 50bp would cost gold about $500. Since Russia's 2022 sanctions, central banks are price-insensitive buyers, which weakened the real yield link. Fast money and CTAs are selling in anticipation of higher yields. Copper at $15,000/t signals policy uncertainty and tight fundamentals rather than slowdown.
items.angle: Gold is down from $5,500-5,600 in January. The thesis has moved from 'fear' to 'debasement', and the debasement bid is the only thing between $4,100 and $3,200.
items.tweetA: Gold is $840 above what real yields and the dollar say it should be. That premium is entirely central bank price-insensitive buying. Take away the bid, and fair value is $3,200. $GLD
items.tweetB: Real yields at 2007 levels, DXY above 102, and gold still near $4,100. Either the central bank bid is carrying it or the model is broken. A $500 drop for 50bp in real yields is the risk. Position accordingly.

items.source: David Lin Report / Jeff Christian (CPM Group)
items.title: Christian: only about 28 of 200 central banks bought gold this year; 1978-80 saw rates, dollar and gold all rise
items.idea: Christian says gold fell from $5,500-5,600 in January to about $4,100, but rising rates and a rising dollar rose with gold together from 1978 to 1980. Only about 28 of roughly 200 central banks bought this year and only a handful in size; they are value buyers who would buy more at $4,100 than at $4,500-4,700. A 5% nominal rate with 3.4% inflation is a 1.6% real rate, and investors typically wait for 3%+ real returns before they stop buying gold.
items.angle: This directly contradicts the 'central banks will always bid' framing in Shiels's piece, and offers a 3% real yield threshold as the level that actually matters.
items.tweetA: Only 28 of ~200 central banks bought gold this year. The 'central banks will bid forever' story is a handful of buyers. If you are long gold on that thesis, check your assumptions before $4,100 becomes $3,600.
items.tweetB: In 1978-80, rates, the dollar and gold all rose together. People forget. Real yield of 1.6% is not the threshold; Christian says investors want 3%. We are a long way from the level that ends the trade.

items.title: Vermeulen: 10-year to 6.5% then 8% in a technical scenario, but he stays long equities and sees BTC to 94.5k
items.idea: Vermeulen says charts point to a 10-year at 6.5% first and potentially 8%, which would likely cause a global financial crisis. A move above 6% could start to hurt equities. He is long on a panic-selling indicator above 3, expecting 3-5% gains within the week and Nasdaq to 35,100. Gold could fall to $3,100, and Bitcoin has turned bullish with a Fibonacci target at about 94,500 as money rotates from metals to crypto if the dollar rises.
items.angle: A trader long equities while forecasting an 8% 10-year is a useful sentiment marker: nobody is positioned for the rate scenario they themselves describe.
items.tweetA: Vermeulen: 10-year to 8% would cause a global financial crisis. Also Vermeulen: still long equities. That gap between what people say and what they hold is the market right now.
items.tweetB: BTC briefly topped $87,000 after the jobs report. Vermeulen has $94,500 as a target on the dollar rising. A dollar-up regime has not been good for crypto historically; this is the one to watch. $BTC

items.source: David Lin Report / Raymond James, St. Louis Fed, Kashkari
items.title: AI capex now exceeds Big Tech operating cash flow; data center construction +$51B while other construction -$120B
items.idea: Raymond James says Big Tech capex began to exceed operating cash flow in Q2. St. Louis Fed data show data center construction up $51B since December 2023 while all other private construction fell $120B. Minneapolis Fed's Kashkari said the AI buildout is likely pushing up the neutral interest rate.
items.angle: A Fed official saying AI raises r-star is a regime change in the framework: capex is no longer a sector story but a determinant of the policy rate. The crowding-out is already visible in construction data.
items.tweetA: Data center construction +$51B since Dec 2023. Everything else private construction: -$120B. Kashkari says AI is lifting the neutral rate. The buildout is not just consuming capital, it is crowding out the rest of the economy.
items.tweetB: Big Tech capex exceeds operating cash flow as of Q2 per Raymond James. Free cash flow is negative at the margin for the sector that is 45% of the S&P. The funding gap is what the SPVs and bond deals are for. $MSFT $GOOGL $AMZN $META

items.title: G7 agrees to release up to 100M barrels over four months; US sends 9,000 troops and a third carrier group
items.idea: On Friday the G7 agreed to release up to 100M barrels of crude and diesel over four months, with a large diesel release in the first 20 days, and Macron said members pledged no export bans; US diesel futures fell as much as 5.6%. Trump rejected Tehran's seven-day Hormuz plan, said he could step up strikes after the midterms, and sent about 9,000 troops aboard warships including a third carrier group. Brent settled at $102.25, WTI $91.11. Kpler puts Hormuz flows at 77% of prewar levels.
items.angle: The policy path is explicitly political: diesel $6.39/gal (down from a $6.53 record) is a midterm issue and the export-ban question is a coin flip per Johnston.
items.tweetA: G7 releases 100M barrels and diesel falls 5.6%. Same day: 9,000 more US troops and a third carrier group head to the region. One hand sells reserves, the other moves toward escalation. That is not a coherent supply policy. $USO $XLE
items.tweetB: Trump says the war ends right after the midterms 'or sooner'. A president who says he could step up strikes if no deal, and also promises diesel relief before the election. The market will price both, and the second will lose.

items.title: The Economist on effective altruism: 'only they can be trusted with the technology' is the alarming idea
items.idea: The Economist calls EA this century's biggest idea, but argues that EAs in Silicon Valley who think only they can be trusted with powerful AI are making the same single-objective mistake they warn about: a small group optimizing for one fatally wrong objective. Alexander Berger of Coefficient Giving has a brief response.
items.angle: The EA-to-AI-lab pipeline is also a governance story: the same people write the safety frameworks, fund the labs and advise the policy.
items.tweetA: The EA argument for AI safety is that a machine optimizing a single wrong objective is dangerous. The Economist's reply: so is a small group that decides only it can be trusted with the machine. Both are principal-agent problems. Only one of them has a board seat.
items.tweetB: Anthropic's S-1 says 80% of $518B in compute is non-cancellable. EA-aligned labs are now locked into trillion-dollar commitments by their own thesis that compute is the constraint. Safety is going to meet the fixed charge, and I know which one wins.

items.title: Anthropic consults theologians on machine consciousness; the Pope's encyclical says AIs do not undergo experiences
items.idea: NYT reports Anthropic has consulted religious scholars on machine consciousness and prioritises questions of consciousness and personhood more than other AI companies. Its team reportedly proposed withdrawing from a Vatican event before the Pope's encyclical Magnifica Humanitas argued AIs 'do not undergo experiences, do not possess a body, do not feel joy or pain... nor do they have a moral conscience.' Exponential View will cover consciousness tomorrow.
items.angle: Model welfare and religion may become a regulatory input. If major religious institutions define AI personhood, that becomes a lobbying surface, and a brand risk for labs.
items.tweetA: The Vatican has an encyclical saying AIs do not feel pain or have a moral conscience. Anthropic is asking theologians whether its models might. One of those two positions will shape the regulatory conversation, and neither is a technical one.
items.tweetB: A frontier lab consults theologians, and a Pope writes an encyclical on AI, in the same quarter as a $518B compute S-1. The industry is simultaneously the biggest capex story on earth and a metaphysics debate. Watch which one the regulators pick up.

items.title: Logan Wright: China's financial system that powered growth now constrains it
items.idea: Logan Wright, a top China macro expert, says the financial system behind China's extraordinary growth is now the constraint, and the old US-China economic rivalry framing no longer fits. Brad Setser and Jordan Schneider push back on whether Xi cares, whether export and supply-chain dominance can sustain growth, and whether AI and EVs can pull China out. Also covered: China's jobs crisis and what the slowdown means for the world.
items.angle: Read against the BMO export-price data: China exporting inflation is a sign that the deflationary-export model is changing, not growing.
items.tweetA: Wright: the financial system that built China's growth is now what holds it back. Setser: exports can keep it going. If exports can do it, why is China's import bill up 21% and its export margin squeezed? The model has a terms-of-trade problem.
items.tweetB: China's export prices +11.6%, import prices +21.0%, a jobs crisis, and an economy where the old financial plumbing no longer allocates well. The world assumed a China slowdown means cheaper goods. That is no longer obviously true.

items.source: ChinaTalk / WarTalk, Ethan Kessler, Garrett Berntsen
items.title: Taiwan drones, the 'Potemkin Pacific' and the Pentagon's bureaucracy
items.idea: Ethan Kessler asks in two parts whether Taiwan can build the drones it needs. WarTalk's 'Potemkin Pacific' argues the US military is trying to cover an enormous ocean with a rather less enormous number of ships. Garrett Berntsen argues that giving government AI is not enough if the institutions using it do not change.
items.angle: The US is moving a third carrier group and 9,000 troops to the Middle East at the same time Pacific coverage is thin: a force-allocation story with commodity implications.
items.tweetA: A third US carrier group just went to the Gulf. WarTalk's argument is that the Pacific is already covered by a force too small for the ocean. Every ship in the Gulf is a ship not in the Taiwan Strait. Markets price Hormuz; nobody prices the opportunity cost.
items.tweetB: Taiwan needs drones, the Pentagon's procurement is a bureaucracy problem, and AI adoption fails without institutional change. The real constraint in defense tech is organizational, not technological. Think about which defense names are paid for process rather than product.

items.title: Inside Chinese AI discourse: a DeepSeek researcher's vision ranges from communist abundance to Cyberpunk 2077
items.idea: Irene Zhang goes inside Chinese AI discourse, where one DeepSeek researcher's vision of an AI future ranges from communist abundance to Cyberpunk 2077, and where Western AI safety and containment rhetoric can sound like an attack on Chinese development, making cooperation harder as stakes rise. The issue also flags China's robotics boom and its answer to Starlink.
items.angle: Export controls framed as 'safety' land as containment in Beijing. That undermines the cooperation channel just as capability gaps narrow.
items.tweetA: In Beijing, Western AI safety talk reads as a containment strategy. In Washington, containment is the safety strategy. Neither side can cooperate on a problem that each describes in the other's threat language.
items.tweetB: China's robotics boom, a Starlink competitor, and a DeepSeek researcher imagining abundance or cyberpunk. The AI race is not one race. China is racing on embodied AI and satellites while the US races on compute.

items.title: Trump expected to name DNI Jay Clayton as AI czar while remaining DNI
items.idea: Per CNN, Trump is expected to name DNI Jay Clayton as his new AI czar, with Clayton staying on as DNI.
items.angle: Intelligence and AI policy under one person: export controls, model security and surveillance become one portfolio. Noahpinion's piece notes Trump's stalling of AI regulation; this is a personnel signal on where it goes.
items.tweetA: The AI czar is also the Director of National Intelligence. Chips, model weights and surveillance all sit with the person who runs the spy agencies. That is a security-first AI policy. Export controls just got a more senior owner. $NVDA $AMD
items.tweetB: One person, two jobs: DNI and AI czar. Either AI policy is now a national security matter in practice, or the czar role is a title. Watch whether the next chip export rule comes from Commerce or from the intelligence community.

items.title: Meta: six papers on open math problems solved by mathematicians working with Muse Spark 1.1/1.2
items.idea: Meta shared six papers on open math problems solved by mathematicians working with Muse Spark 1.1 and 1.2 in Thinking Mode through the regular meta.ai chat. Meta also released Muse Gadgets, an open-source ESP32 firmware and Linux SDK for building hardware that works with Muse.
items.angle: Open problems solved in a consumer chat interface, not a research cluster: capability diffusion to normal users. Muse on ESP32 hardware is the edge-device angle.
items.tweetA: Six open math problems solved by mathematicians using a chat window on meta.ai. Not a cluster, not a special build. The distance between frontier research capability and a consumer product is now zero. $META
items.tweetB: Muse on an ESP32 chip, the cheapest microcontroller there is. Meta is going after hardware makers, not just app developers. The platform war is moving from phones to $5 boards.

items.title: Gemini Desktop gets Full Access permission; DeepSeek Harness v0.2 ships a desktop agent; Cactus Whistle is 16.9MB
items.idea: Gemini Desktop is getting a Full Access permission for computer use, letting it read, modify or delete files anywhere on a Mac and control other apps without asking each time (still hidden). DeepSeek Harness v0.2 is live on macOS, Windows and Linux with Plugins and Workspaces. Cactus released Whistle, a 16.9MB speech-to-text model that runs on CPU and mostly beats Whisper base with 9x less file size and 6x speed. Maket 2.0 generates floor plans and 3D views from a prompt.
items.angle: Agent permissions are the new OS-level security boundary. A 16.9MB speech model on CPU is the edge inference cost curve falling.
items.tweetA: Gemini Desktop is testing a permission to read, modify or delete any file on your Mac without asking. DeepSeek ships a desktop agent the same week. The question for enterprise IT is not capability, it is who signs for the blast radius. $GOOGL
items.tweetB: A 16.9MB speech model that beats Whisper base on CPU with 6x speed. Inference is leaving the data center for the phone and the microcontroller. The marginal cost of voice transcription just went to zero for anyone who ships software.

items.title: Volantis raises $88M Series A to attack AI's memory bottleneck with photonics
items.idea: Volantis raised an $88M Series A co-led by Lachy Groom and Abstract, with John Doerr, Susa Ventures, VXI Capital and Triatomic Capital participating, to tackle AI's memory bottleneck with photonics. Also: David Robinson, who worked on OpenAI's Safety Systems team and led policy planning, left OpenAI last week.
items.angle: Photonics for memory is the next layer after photonics for networking. A Series A of this size indicates the market expects the memory wall to bind before the interconnect wall.
items.tweetA: $88M Series A for photonic memory. Everyone owns optical networking. Almost nobody owns optical memory. Doerr and Groom think the wall is next. $COHR $LITE $MU
items.tweetB: OpenAI's safety policy lead left last week; a photonics memory startup raised $88M this week. One is a people signal about governance, the other is a capital signal about hardware bottlenecks. Only one has a price tag.

items.title: Trump's second term as a 'world-historic failure': approval at lows, prediction markets favor Democrats in both chambers
items.idea: Smith argues the second Trump presidency has failed in the court of public opinion: approval is at historic lows going into the midterms, Republicans now disapprove on cost of living, and a growing number of 2024 Trump voters say they never voted for him. Prediction markets are increasingly sure Democrats take the House and give them a better-than-even chance of the Senate. Trump has promised $5,000 checks if Republicans win, which is reportedly driving voters away. Peter Thiel is distancing himself.
items.angle: The midterm result changes the fiscal and tariff path, which matters for the long end: a Democratic House is a check on spending but also on tariffs. Hay thinks Trump contests a Democratic sweep.
items.tweetA: Prediction markets give Democrats the House and better-than-even odds at the Senate. Trump promises $5,000 checks if Republicans win. The bond market just printed 5.6% on the 30-year. The checks are a $1.5T promise into a bond-buyer strike.
items.tweetB: Midterms are four weeks away, the October FOMC is a week before them, and Warsh has to choose between a hike and the president. The Fed calendar and the political calendar overlap by design. Rates volatility is a political variable.

charts.desc: Trump approval, cost-of-living by party, GOP-vs-Trump support, prediction markets for House/Senate, trust-on-economy polls

items.title: South Korea lets stocks, bonds and funds move onchain from Feb 2027; its depository builds on Avalanche
items.idea: South Korea unveiled rules letting stocks, bonds and funds move onchain from February 2027, with its securities depository building connectivity on Avalanche. SMBC Nikko, one of Japan's largest securities firms, is building a trading venue on Uniswap with compliance inside a hook, to launch mid-2027. IMF approved a $138M disbursement to El Salvador under its $1.4B EFF, waiving the breach of bitcoin accumulation limits.
items.angle: Two Asian incumbents choose public rails (Avalanche, Uniswap) rather than private chains. The IMF waiving El Salvador's bitcoin limit shows that the conditionality is soft.
items.tweetA: South Korea's securities depository is building on Avalanche. A major Japanese broker is building on Uniswap with compliance in a hook. Incumbent market structure is moving to public chains in 2027. $AVAX $UNI
items.tweetB: The IMF waived El Salvador's breach of its bitcoin accumulation limit and paid out $138M. The lesson for every other sovereign: the program conditionality is negotiable if the program is large enough.

items.title: Tokenized equities scale: 26 new stocks on Base, BNB Chain passes $1B, Fiserv puts a bank coin on Solana
items.idea: 26 new tokenized stocks landed on Base, tradable 24/7. BNB Chain became the first chain to surpass $1B in tokenized stocks and ETFs. PUSA, the onchain common stock of Powerus, went live on Solana via Sunrise, issued by Backpack Securities and redeemable one to one for the Nasdaq-listed share. Fiserv's digital asset platform went live with Bank of North Dakota's dollar-backed coin on Solana, covering 90+ banks and credit unions. BNY was reported in talks with Payward (Kraken).
items.angle: Tokenized equities are competing on chains, not on regulation. Fiserv reaching 90+ banks gives the stablecoin side a distribution channel without Circle or Tether.
items.tweetA: BNB Chain tokenized stocks pass $1B. 26 more equities on Base. Fiserv puts a bank stablecoin in front of 90 banks. The 24/7 equity market is being built by chains and core processors, not by exchanges. $NDAQ $ICE $COIN
items.tweetB: Fiserv is a core processor. When Bank of North Dakota issues a coin on Solana through them, 90+ community banks get the rails at once. The distribution channel for stablecoins was never going to be crypto-native.

items.title: Chainalysis: $387M Bitget hack is DPRK; Aave Loop Safe Module exploited; Core Lightning patch warning
items.idea: Chainalysis attributed the $387M Bitget hack to DPRK actors, with funds moved across Ethereum, XRP, Zcash and Tron. Aave v3 Loop Safe Module was exploited for about 114.09 ETH via an access-control flaw in FlashLoopAdapter, per SlowMist. Core Lightning warned operators on 26.06.7 or earlier to upgrade immediately as attackers targeted unpatched nodes. Near announced $3.8M stolen in the NEAR Intents exploit was returned in full. bitFlyer starts a 48-hour transfer cooldown after JPY deposits on October 15.
items.angle: DPRK routing through Zcash is a notable shift; privacy chains are now part of the laundering path. bitFlyer's cooldown is a regulatory response to account-takeover patterns.
items.tweetA: $387M, DPRK, and the funds moved through Zcash. Privacy chains are now in the laundering path, which puts pressure on every exchange listing ZEC. $ZEC
items.tweetB: Aave module exploit via access control, Core Lightning nodes under active attack, bitFlyer adds a 48-hour cooling-off after deposits. The attack surface is not smart contracts anymore, it is permissions and operations.

items.title: Silicon Exchange launches GPU cluster financing on Stripe, Tempo, Privy and OUSD; Forward Industries holds 8.5M SOL
items.idea: Silicon Exchange launched GPU cluster financing for AI compute, built on Stripe, Tempo, Privy and OUSD. Forward Industries added nearly 949,000 SOL last quarter at an average cost of $83, bringing holdings to 8.5M SOL, roughly 1.4% of circulating supply. Tether-backed Utexo plans to launch USDT on Bitcoin this month using RGB; Copper launched institutional access to Hyperliquid perps.
items.angle: GPU financing on stablecoin rails is the crypto version of the SPV leasing structures in the AI credit piece. Treasury companies at 1.4% of supply are a concentration risk.
items.tweetA: GPU cluster financing built on a stablecoin payment stack. The same week Amazon explores an $8B GPU leaseback. Credit for compute is being built on two rails at once, one regulated and one not. $AMZN $SOL
items.tweetB: Forward Industries owns 1.4% of all SOL at an average cost of $83. Treasury companies are the new concentrated holders. When their equity trades below NAV, the coin has a forced seller.

items.title: Blast L2 shuts down, Anchorage lays off 17%, Lido cuts EarnUSD fees from 1%+10% to 0.2%+15%
items.idea: Blast L2 announced its shutdown over unsustainable costs, with users required to withdraw to Ethereum before October 26. Anchorage Digital laid off 17% of staff. Lido EarnUSD cut its fee cap to 0.5% AUM + 20% performance, launching at 0.2% AUM + 15%, down from 1% AUM + 10%. New York and Wyoming regulators agreed to jointly oversee crypto firms.
items.angle: L2 consolidation: a venture-funded L2 closes because costs exceed revenue. Fee compression at Lido is the yield-product version of the same pressure.
items.tweetA: Blast is shutting down because it can't cover its costs. Lido cuts management fees from 1% to 0.2%. Crypto infrastructure is going through a margin collapse, the same way SaaS went through one. Survivors need scale. $ETH $LDO
items.tweetB: A custodian lays off 17% while regulators from NY and Wyoming agree to share exam data and fast-track licenses for established firms. Crypto's regulatory moat is rising while the revenue pool shrinks. Incumbents win both ways.

items.title: MacroEdge: SPR release is 'unsustainable'; Saudi-Yemen escalation risk; Europe could back out of the release
items.idea: MacroEdge says the G7/IEA SPR release was expected for weeks and is part of a 'patience through October' view: the last month where such announcements move energy prices, especially if conflict escalates. He flags that Europe could back out after Trump said he never planned an export ban, and that a Saudi invasion of Yemen with a conscripted force would be one of the biggest military blunders in modern war and could last years. He calls subsidizing demand with strategic reserves while refineries are bombed unsustainable, and says Hormuz at 'pre-war flows' is doublespeak.
items.angle: Contradicts Hunter's 'oil has peaked' view: this is the bull case from the same week, with Saudi infrastructure exposed to the Houthis.
items.tweetA: MacroEdge: October is the last month SPR announcements move the oil price. Hunter says oil peaked. Hay says $200 is not outlandish. Three views, one data point: the buffers are the story. Once they run out, the options are demand destruction or price. $XLE
items.tweetB: A Saudi-Yemen ground war would put the largest oil exporter's own infrastructure inside the war zone. Houthis can already hit Saudi energy assets at will. The risk is not only supply, it is who underwrites the insurance on that infrastructure.

items.title: 'The growth engine has become nominal inflation with data centers stacked on top'
items.idea: MacroEdge, in a rant, argues the missing US 'growth engine' he warned about in February has become nominal inflation with data centers on top, which looks like a miracle after 2007 but is more likely a mirage as 2027 arrives. He compares policy trajectory to Argentina, Zimbabwe and Venezuela headlines, says equities rising on a nominal basis is not inherently positive, and says labor data will show more signal as the workforce ages. He stopped publishing data center construction data after drawing heat from that crowd.
items.angle: This lines up with the St. Louis Fed numbers: +$51B data center construction vs -$120B other. Hanke's money growth point supplies the mechanism.
items.tweetA: Nominal GDP up, data center capex up, equities up. Strip out the inflation and the AI build, and what's left? The St. Louis Fed says other private construction is -$120B since 2023. The 'growth engine' is one sector wearing the rest of the economy's capital.
items.tweetB: Equities at records with the 30-year at 5.6%, in a regime where policy is aimed at nominal stimulus. In every historical example I can think of, that ends with the bond market setting the terms. We are in the part where it is still being negotiated.

charts.desc: Argentina equity vs inflation, Zimbabwe analog, Brent reaction; charts inside

items.title: Primary research priced at $30/yr as an anti-bot filter; $699 Inner Circle tier; shift from nano-caps to small caps
items.idea: Hermit says it will cut cadence to 1-2 posts per week from 2027 and move the annual subscription to Substack's $30 minimum, explicitly as a filter against scrapers and bot crawlers rather than for profit, with a $699/year Inner Circle for 1-on-1 management access. Its interviews with management are the 'primary data' it argues AI cannot replicate. It reports up 10%+ YTD and says it is outgrowing nano-caps to hunt in better-known small caps; it will publish a Naked Wines ($WINE) deep dive and a TSS Inc. ($TSSI) note.
items.angle: Pricing as an anti-scraper filter is a new media-economics pattern: price floor to exclude bots. Also an example of newsletters positioning around primary access as the AI-proof asset.
items.tweetA: A newsletter prices at $30 a year not to earn money, but to keep scrapers out. Primary-source management interviews are what AI can't copy. The paywall is now an anti-bot device. Expect more of this. Next step: proof-of-human subscriptions.
items.tweetB: Two-tier: $30 for the write-ups, $699 for the person. The value is moving from analysis (which AI produces) to access (which it can't). Same logic as a sell-side analyst's real product being the call, not the note.

items.title: 'My Fuji and Happiness Code': a Japanese film on inter-generational households, coffee as a vocation
items.idea: A review of a Japanese film in which a college student moves in with his grandmother and learns his late grandfather had secretly enrolled her in the same college as an anniversary present. The author's observation: 'we are meant to live in inter-generational households.' The student realizes his future lies in his love of coffee: 'The chances of finding something you love isn't that high.'
items.angle: Inter-generational living and specialty coffee as a career: both are demographic and consumer signals in aging societies. Hermit's piece in the same batch invests in specialty coffee.
items.tweetA: A Japanese film about a student moving in with his grandmother, who goes to the same college. Multi-generational housing is back in the data across the US, Japan and Southern Europe. It is a response to housing costs and an aging population, and nobody prices it.
items.tweetB: Two newsletters in the same hour pitch specialty coffee: one as a film plot, one as an investment. Consumers are paying up for craft at the low end of the price ladder while real retail sales go sideways (Snider). Small luxuries are what is left of discretionary spend.
